image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

|---|---|---|

| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |

1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |
raw_comment:
I notice that nearly every state shifted blue in 2008, but then gradually shifted red in 2012 and 2016 and slightly back to the left for 2020--but not as far as in 2008. 

I wonder what this graph would look like without the electoral college. 

My state has (with the exception of Clinton, Carter, and Johnson) rarely crossed party lines since the 1930s (around the party switch; TN follows the same trend with the opposite party prior to the 40s). Since my political alignment is the opposite of how my state normally votes, the electoral college renders my vote virtually meaningless. 

Catchy Headline:
Partisanship Comes In Waves: A Visual Representation of Electoral Trends from 2004 to 2020

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment:
Headline: The States Are Covering the Spread...Sadly
1. I’m particularly noticing how spread out all of these states are right now compared to what they were in 2004. This indicates that states are starting to shift farther from a balance between republican and democrats, becoming strongholds by the year. The spread of states from a tie indicates how polarized our country is becoming, since each state is becoming strongly associated with one party or another. Therefore, our elections are constantly being decided by the few swing states. Only these states have a major influence due to the landslides every year in other states. I hope the parties won’t give up on trying to flip a state even if it seems out of reach. I also hope voters believe their vote makes a difference. Then all 50 states will contribute to electing future presidents. 
2. 
I wonder if parties will still spend time trying to win the voters of the states they had but now have lost. I think they should absolutely do so. Georgia was out of reach for Democrats in 2004 but has flipped blue in this most recent election. With this strategy both parties can win back states they previously had. 
3. 
Being from Boston, this will likely have a miniscule effect on my state. Massachusetts hasn’t flipped red since Regan and they have been shifting more left ever since. What I will say is that in General Presidential Elections, candidates will likely not campaign in Mass., for it is almost guaranteed Mass. will go blue.

raw_comment:
Tying US History with these 5 recent presidents I see that G. W. Bush came in with his 2nd term with several states supporting him following 9/11 leaving the country in a state of shock. B. Obama came strong with the amount of supporters pushing to make history by adding the first African American towards presidency. America slowly began to lean Republican following 2012 election. 2016 D. J. Trump came forward and turned the board to lean towards him causing many states to start pedaling red. With the country now split, red states leaned blue and J. R. Biden grabs the win.
I question if a Democrat trend will appear after Biden's' term is over? if so how will it affect morals for the people and will they remain strong Democrats or question their ideals.
While I don't really see my community changing much, that the possibility of seeing Democrat policies affecting an already blue city in Texas. While effects might be positive there are always concern of the negative effects to already underlying issues.
Finally you will notice many states taking "U" turns while other states slow turns but never staying near the same path. Similar to a person walking tipsy I choose to call it "The States Drunk walk" .

raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph shows the difference in party shifts in the United States for the past 5 presidential elections using red snd blue lines. I noticed that both lines bent towards the democratic party in 2004-2008, depicting that people don’t always vote “red or blue” every year, but select different candidates depending on their ideologic preferences, not just a default side. The following years illustrate the same concept, that democrats don’t always vote blue and republicans don’t always vote red, but both parties for the candidate with political philosophy and plans most aligning to their own, often independent of “red” or “blue.”
I wonder why in 2012,  some states voted almost completely republicans and others almost completely democratic.  I wonder if the further division caused by the media was a factor in why the 2020 election had some states exceptionally blue and others exceptionally red. I also wonder why states like Utah, Hawaii, and North Carolina had such a fluid change in the voting in these elections.
An impact that this could have is thats it is less likely for more worthy candidates to run for president given the amount of backlash they receive, republican or democrat. It’s also less likely that there will be as many voters next election because this year, neither candidate was liked very much; most people said they had to choose the “lesser of two evils.” 
Catchy Headline:  Swinging Left and Right

raw_comment: I noticed that republicans and democrats have wavered over the years to each others parties. I wonder what makes them change their parties so easily. What impact this has on me and my community is that if people are willing to change parties so easily, then when it comes down to voting for representatives, presidents, mayors, etc, it's up to the merit of the people who are running and how well they influence people to vote for them. A catchy hook for this graph would be "Red vs. Blue".

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

What do you notice in this graph?

Something I notice going on the graph is how there were more state votes for the Democratic Party instead of for the Republican Party. In the graph we see how many states that were once voters of the Republican Party have now changed to voting for the Democratic Party.


What do you wonder?

Something I wonder is how during the  past years states have changed their voting towards the Democratic Party. What changed the way some states voted or why did some states suddenly chose to vote for the Democratic Party.



What impact does this have on you and your community?

One impact this has on me is when I’m able to vote I will be able to observe the two opinions that each state has differently according to its political party selection. The different types of political beliefs that different states have chosen and for the states that were once considered to be part of a certain political party have now changed to another. This impacts our community and society because though one side might agree with one political party, the other might agree with other which then leads to less people wanting to unite and find a solution that both can agree on. This also leads to violence and not much of unity. After a while of arguments and destruction of the country.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that most of the state's voters were in the same party throughout the years. However they did lean towards a certain side. Several swing states switched over to another party during the past few elections. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what caused voters to switch sides. What change brought on switching parties?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts me and my community because the decision to choose a president is in the hands of the public although some believe otherwise.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
The graph shows how voting by party has shifted in the 50 states for the past 5 presidential elections. During the years 2004 to 2008, a lot of the democratic states have gotten more democratic and less republican. A catchy headline would be "Red or Blue this year?"

raw_comment:
I noticed the change within this graph became very different during Obama’s 2 elections compared to all of the 5 shown. It looks like the blue states during 2008 and 2012 voted more dramatically for the democratic candidate than other years and the red states during these elections voted more dramatically for the republican candidate compared to the other years. I wonder why this happened. Did it have to do with the state of the US at the time or was there another reason? I think this impacts my community because the way a state flips can seriously affect who wins an election.

The graph shows that in recent years, people are not as one-sided in their political view than other year, creating a more centered and balance environment in America. raw_comment:
Title: Intricacies of American Politics Made Visual 

Context makes the graph all the more intriguing. Obama (in 2008) was able to increase the margin of victory in HI by a startling 35 points; so too was Mitt Romney (in 2012) able to increase the margin of victory in UT by a likewise startling 20 points. Obama is a HI native; Romney, the first Mormon to head a major party presidential ticket, hails from UT, the only Mormon-majority state. The prospect of "one of your own" in the White House caused Hawaiians and Utahans to turn out in record numbers. This begs the question: in the "United States" of America, why might your identity as a citizen of a state trump your identity as an American? Does love of state top love of country? In an age where voter turnout teeters around a measly 50%, Republicans and Democrats alike need to analyze the intricacy of factors that drive voter turnout up or down. Americans like to boast a rational electorate, but this may not be so. In an increasingly contentious political atmosphere, it's important to analyze how a voter's personal identity and sense of reason intersect to manifest as a vote for either candidate. The concept of identity is central to every human being and everything that human does; politics is no exception to this, for better or worse.

raw_comment:
Title: A New Type of Art: Intricacies of American Politics Made Visual 

Context makes the graph all the more intriguing. Obama (in 2008) was able to increase the margin of victory in HI by a startling 35 points; so too was Mitt Romney (in 2012) able to increase the margin of victory in UT by a likewise startling 20 points. Obama is a HI native; Romney, the first Mormon to head a major party presidential ticket, hails from UT, the only Mormon-majority state. The prospect of "one of your own" in the White House caused Hawaiians and Utahans to turn out in record numbers. This begs the question: in the "United States" of America, why might your identity as a citizen of a state trump your identity as an American? Does love of state top love of country? In an age where voter turnout teeters around a measly 50%, Republicans and Democrats alike need to analyze the intricacy of factors that drive voter turnout up or down. Americans like to boast a rational electorate, but this may not be so. In an increasingly contentious political atmosphere, it's important to analyze how a voter's personal identity and sense of reason intersect to manifest as a vote for either candidate. The concept of identity is central to every human being and everything that human does; politics is no exception to this, for better or worse.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment: After looking at the New York Times graph from January 13 2021 we noticed that the blue line for the democratic candidates is stretched far out in the year 2012. We also notice that there are multiple states being connected by the same line. Another thing we noticed is that voting by the party has varied in the past couple of years. We thought it was interesting that in 2008 there was a big swing left and many republicans voted for Barack Obama. We wonder why a lot of republicans that had voted for Obama decided not to in 2012. After 2012 it started to even out again. One thing we wonder is why republican votes seem to be inconsistent and we wonder if they will continue to vary as time goes on. This impacts our community because helps visualize the side people are leaning towards and patterns that are being created.  The catchy headline we would use is “Swing to the Left, Swing to the Right”.

raw_comment: I notice that in the 2004 election Hawaii was less than +10 Democrat but then in 2008 they were over +40 Democrat. I noticed that a lot of voters swayed to voting for Obama in the election of 2008, even though some of the states had been barely Democratic or had voted Republican. Immediately, I noticed the huge sway of voters in Obama's favor.   I noticed that within the past 5 elections, there have been many states that have flipped from conservative to democratic. I wonder what about Utah makes it such a republican state. I wonder what makes Utah stay consistently on the deep Republican side. I wonder what it was that made the states switch and why there aren’t as many states that have flipped over to conservative. This impacts our community because it shows how the people around us have voted for the past 5 elections. The impact this may potentially have on our community is what policies affect certain groups of people, as Republicans push things for some groups and Demcratics push other things for others. This impacts our community because it allows us to see as a state how we have voted in the past 5 elections compared to other states.  A title for this graph could be, “How states sway, voter edition”, “How Things Have Changes in the Past Five Presidential Elections”, “Voting Behaviors: The Election Flips and Flops Around All the Time!”.  “How did your state vote?”.

raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed in the graph was that it seemed very chaotic, with voting seeming to be generally in favor of Democrat candidates and eventually shifting toward somewhat of a more equal middle ground. The one thing I wonder though is why this trend happened? With Obama's seemingly overwhelming support via votes, wouldn't it be reasonable to guess that he could accomplish a lot and have a high approval rating, keeping that trend going for the next presidents? What specifically happened during that presidency that led people to reconsider their choices, and according to votes drastically shift the balance towards a more 50/50 split? Within my community, I don't necessarily think this graph affects it. My state has historically tended to vote based on the most populous city and as such our voting if put on a graph would be a straight line. However, I do think within a smaller community this graph has an impact as it gets people starting to wonder why these trends are happening and what is driving them. 

For my headline, I would choose: "The political shifts; From majority to split"

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is how chaotic this graph looks. Then the light blue lines, dark blue, dark red, and light red lines. Looking at the graph there are a lot of lines representing states and where their stance is and how it shifts or doesn't really throughout 16 years. It is also very interesting to see that the huge switches or the loops that go in and out throughout the different years. I wonder why there are such huge changes between the years. I wonder why there are such huge changes from stats that choose +40 reps to almost at a tie. This affects my community and me as from this graph we are able to tell which states vote towards which way in the election. Also as a community, it is very interesting to see which ways the states change based on the year and the president.

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is how chaotic this graph looks. Then the light blue lines, dark blue, dark red, and light red lines. Looking at the graph there are a lot of lines representing states and where their stance is and how it shifts or doesn't really throughout 16 years. It is also very interesting to see that the huge switches or the loops that go in and out throughout the different years. I wonder why there are such huge changes between the years. I wonder why there are such huge changes from stats that choose +40 reps to almost at a tie. This affects my community and me as from this graph we are able to tell which states vote towards which way in the election. Also as a community, it is very interesting to see which ways the states change based on the year and the president.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the votes are unpredictable. In 2004, the number of votes for each party's candidate was almost with there being slightly more Republican voters. In 2008, quite a few states turned blue and voted for Obama. When it came to his reelection in 2012, he had fewer votes as a couple of states turned back to red but still had enough votes to win. However, in 2016, these same swing states turned red. For the 2020 election, some states flipped again and voted blue, while some states remained red. For each party, however, there are states that haven't flipped for any election. 

I wonder what this graph would look like for past elections and what it will look like in the future. I also wonder what characterizes a swing state and what causes it to flip almost every election. Why are they more likely to flip parties each election? In Obama's 2008 election, I wonder what pulled voters in and caused so many states to flip blue. At the same time, I wonder why a couple flipped back to red during his reelection?

This impacts me and my community because it shows just how divided votes are and also how they can change each election. I live in Massachusetts, which is a strong democratic state and unlikely to flip. It's interesting to see how states flip and how the media presents information to the public depending on the party and views of that state. 

A headline could be "Making Waves: Political Party Shifts in Elections (2004-2020)".

raw_comment:
In looking at this graph I notice that during the 2016 election, many normal Democrat voting states turned Republican. I wonder if this party switch was due to the allegations against Hillary Clinton and her potential involvement in illegal business. Throughout her campaign questionable information came out about Hillary, which I assume is the cause for the normally Democrat states turning red. While this impacts my country as it can allow us to somewhat determine how the next elections will go, it does not necessarily my community. New Jersey has always been an extremely Democratic state and never changed even during the 2016 election. 
New Headline, "After the 2016, States Are Turning More Democrat"

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice that most if not all of the lines fluctuate wildly. Most of the states in the center of the graph have switched  between a majority vote for the Democrat to the Republican and visa versa at least once. I also notice that former President Obama pulled multiple republican states and their votes towards the Democratic party, and former President Trump pulled states and their votes towards the Republican party.
I wonder how this graph would look if we went back to the first election. Perhaps the lines might show some states fluctuate even wilder from side to side. I also wonder what the graph would look like if it showed other parties.
I don't know how this could impact my community, but something I do know is that it shows the impact. Colorado has held close to the Democratic party since 2004, which means that it's likely that our state's votes will stay that way.
A title I have for this graph is: Wining in a Landslide: A Seismic Look at America's Votes

raw_comment:
I notice that over the course of the 16 years, voting by party has varied for many states. In 2004, the two sides are almost symmetrical, but if anything, more states had more republican voters. Then in 2008, there was a significant swing to the left, as many states who had a moderate number of Republican voters in 2004, voted for Barack Obama in 2008. Between 2012 and 2020, the two sides mostly evened out again, with some states varying back and forth. In 2020 it appears the lines are starting to pull left again, which makes sense considering Biden won the election and several swing states has voted in his favor. Although the lines are quite curved, which shows they shifted a lot, however, throughout, there are states that stayed strongly to one of either side, showing that recently the country has been extremely divided by political parties. I wonder why Barack Obama so strongly pulled so many voters from swing states and even weak/moderate republican voting states? And why did they swing back to republican voting the next year? This impacts me and my community because it shows how divided our country is and this division has recently been creating a lot of struggles in our country. It's scary because the media in predominantly republican areas displays very different coverage than I get living in Massachusetts, therefore, I feel political parties continue to get even more divided until this problem is solved. 

Waves of Political Party Voting (2004-2020)

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that most of the states that flipped between the years 2004-2020 were more moderate in the 2004 election than the states that did not flip. Between the 2004 and 2008 election, almost every state's votes (even Republican ones) became more Democratic. Between the 2008 and 2012 election, most state's votes became more Republican. In the last two elections (2016 and 2020) the state's votes changed by a smaller degree and more randomly. In the last two elections, there was neither a more Democratic trend nor a more Republican trend between all the states. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why so many more people voted Democratic in the 2008 election, and I wonder why so many more people voted Republican in the 2012 election. Is it because people were unsatisfied with the Presidents of the time? Were they hoping for a more radical change by flipping their votes?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in a state that has voted Democratic since 2004. Since 2004, my state's slightly more Democratic, a fact that I am not surprised by. Thus, party shifting does not impact my community as much as it might impact people in Vermont or Ohio. However, as party views become more one-sided in my state, my community's values tend to surround me in school and on social media.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that a lot of states voted for Bush in 2004, then flipped and voted for Obama in 2008. I also see that in 2008 Obama had a strong majority of the states but in 2012 it was less, but still enough for him to win.  Most of the years there is a clear majority one way or the other but in 2016 and 2020, it is much harder to see a clear majority. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder how the graph would look going back even farther to older presidencies.  

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in Massachusetts, so it is interesting to see some states flip, while Massachusetts is very unlikely to flip from blue to red. 

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
"Flip or Flop, Who Did Your State Vote For?"

raw_comment:
I notice that in the 2008 election of President Barack Obama states that were already blue went more democratic, a couple of swing states that voted red in the 2004 election went blue, and states that voted very republican in the 2004 election shifted more to the left, towards the democrats.

In the 2016 and 2020 election, no states voted very democratic (+40 Dem.). A majority of the states in the 2016 election voted more towards the right and swing states voted republican. I wonder why in each election, except 2012, the president keeps shifting from one party to another party. Maybe it's because people aren't satisfied with the state of the country and think the other party, that's not currently in office, can make life better for Americans.

This effects my community because I live in NJ, a primarily blue state. Although NJ hasn't voted Republican since 1988, I notice a lot of my classmates and a growing amount of people in my community are conservative. It will be interesting to see when/if New Jersey will vote Republican again and what factors will push them towards voting red.

US Elections: Shifting of Political Parties

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Today’s graph shows the shifts of voting by party in the fifty states in the past five presidential elections.  

From 9 am – 2 pm ET today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Plus, please share a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” website, the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs) or 
a slide show of 60 of our favorite graphs (tinyurl.com/NYT60Graphs).  
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

Keep noticing and wondering.  Next week’s graph will be posted by Friday.    The topic – the gaps between Black and white mortality rates for the top 15 causes of death.

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.

|---|---|---|

| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |
raw_comment:
1. I notice that during the years 2004 to 2008, a lot of the democratic states have gotten more democratic and less republican. Many of the republican states in the south also became less republican and more democratic, despite them still being counted as republican states. The following years following 2016-2020, a lot of the blue states became more republican while the republican states continued to become more republican. 
2. I wonder what made the states sway from a democratic lean during 2008-2012 to a more republican lean during 2016-2020. I wonder if it was because the winning candidate's persuasion to have an impact on states votes, or if there was any voter fraud that may have swayed the votes to a certain candidate. 
3. The impact that this has on our community is that it shows where our state falls and the typical values and political beliefs that the people where I live feel. I can see that Massachusetts has always been a democratic state, and has been one of the few to get more democratic throughout the years. This shows that most people here have democratic beliefs. 
4. Possible title: "US Elections: To be More Red or to be More Blue?"

|---|---|---|

| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment:
1. The first thing I notice is the sparsity of data points on the edges of either graph. This makes a decent amount of sense, seeing as most states tend to be more moderate in their voting tendencies, not voting 100% for the same party. There is also a significant dip in data points around the middle tie line. This could be because each state tends to lean more heavily to one party in their voting, rather that having a total tie. 
2. I wonder if this is only for the presidential candidates, or an average of the elections as a whole. Meaning is this just assessing the presidential votes, or also counting each states smaller elections.  
3. I think its a little funny to see Utah having voted completely republican, for Mitt Romney over Obama. The following election, there was a super large push back against the republican candidate. I noticed that Utah in this last election is closer to Dem. than any previous election. 
4. Making Waves: States Flip Sides

raw_comment:
1. I notice a bunch of states flip from one side to the next. 
2. I wonder what they're promising them to get them to flip like that. 
3. These people only have power insofar as everyone respects that they do. From personal experience, a lot of people don't. I suspect this leads to deification of the law in the heads of those who have internalized it, they have made this idea sacred and as such hold it above their own self interest. And as such, power spreads its hold, maintains its legitimacy. 
4. The American people struggle to decide which oligarch will pretend to represent them

raw_comment:
1. The first thing that really stood out to me was the effect of Obama’s 2008 election. Out of the five selected elections, Obama’s 08 was the most far leaning to one side. It appears that Obama’s 08 election was so monumental because he switched many pro republican states to democratic, and already pro democratic states to farther leaning democratic states.
2. I wonder about the future of the republican party. It seems from this data that the Republican party has weaker voters as time goes on. I would say this is because of the influx of younger voters. It is proven that younger votes are more democratic, and as times goes on, I think American will be seeing less and less Republican presidents.
3. This data really doesn’t have much an effect on me, or my community. I live in Illinois, and it is quite apparent that Illinois is a very pro-Democratic state, mainly because of Chicago. I don’t think we will be seeing Illinois go red.
4. It’s clear to me what’s going on in this graph. America is pushing and pushing for democratic candidates. I would title the headline “YOUNG VOTERS PROMOTE A BLUE WAVE.”

| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |

1. Something I noticed while looking at the graph was there was a way bigger push towards the democratic side in 2008 while Obama was running however then in 2012 while Obama was still running there was a very strong push on the republican side. 
2. I wonder what truly creates such a push to a certain side of the person running stays the same such as the years 2008 and then 2012 it was Obama both years yet the way the people sided were so different.

With the way media is now everyone has access to so much with just an easy click of a button which really does play a huge role in which party one votes for.

raw_comment:
1. I’m noticing that some of the red lines are blending into blue lines, although generally blue and red lines seem to be moving in opposite ways until 2020 where they all seem to straighten out a bit more. 

2. I wonder how different the graph would be if it focused on individual parties instead of both democrat and republican as a whole.

3. The impact this has is that it shows the tide of american politics and if it depends on parties as a whole rather than the political candidates over the years that have gone by. 

4. The Tides of a Political Ocean

1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.

|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |

| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

1. What do you notice: The first thing that I notice after glancing at the graph is that the country swayed a lot to the left in 2008, but then swayed back a little more to the middle in 2012, and then more to the right in 2016 and back towards the middle again in 2020. Overall the Democratic side had been pretty consistently to the far left but lately it appears more are shifting right. And the Republican side had been slowly moving left but lately there had been a lot of back and forth and now more centered again.
2. What do you wonder: I wonder why there is so much drastic switching between parties. I understand that there will always be some change, but it surprises me how much of a shift there was especially in 2008 and 2020.
3. What impact does this have on you and your community: For me personally, living in Illinois, there hasn’t been too much rightward shifting as Illinois is a predominantly democratic state. However, for swing states, it shows how much shifting is going on which is a big deal because their votes are very crucial to deciding each election.
4. What’s going on in this graph: This graph illustrates the change in voting pattern for either party each state had for every election in the past 16 years.
Headline: “Swing to the Left, Swing to the Right”

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment:
1. The first thing I noticed about this graph was the inconsistencies regarding the Republican party. Their voting over the years has clearly flipped and has little to no pattern regarding its votes. However, the Democratic party had, for the most part, stayed together and consistent, usually voting for the same candidate as their fellow democrats. 
2. I wonder why the Republican party is so inconsistent with their voting history. How have Republicans inconsistent voting history reflected the recent election, as this is the first year in a while that the incumbent hasn't won a second term. 
3. This does not have a huge impact on my specific community because I live in a blue state that has consistently voted democratic for many consecutive years. However, as a nation, this affects us greatly because it shows the inconsistencies and the inability to truly predict who will win elections, as states are prone to flip frequently. 
4. In this graph, it shows the flipped voters, primarily on the Republican side. I would name this article "A Decade of Party Flips".

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment:
What do you notice: Glancing at the middle of the graph, I immediately notice the large wave of states favoring the Democratic Party - likely due to the popularization of Barack Obama’s campaign in 2008.

What do you wonder: I wonder if there are patterned socioeconomic environments in the states that regularly vote either Republican or Democratic. 

Impact: This graph does not have much of a personal impact due to Illinois, my home state, being a Democratic state throughout the timeline of this graph. However, I feel that this graph has more of an effect on the community as it debunks and clarifies some of the myths and chaos of the recent elections; or transforms reality into a humbling, quantitative matter at a minimum.

Graph Summary: This graph by the New York Times displays the electoral tendencies of each United State, while also quantifying the “closeness”, alias competitiveness of each Presidential race from 2004-2020.

Headline: “The Realities of the U.S. Presidental Race”

   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment:
1. I notice that this graph is looking at presidential election margins from the past 5 years. It seems as if some states have flipped back and forth quite a bit 
2. I would be interested to compare this to election turn out data broken down by the state in each of these elections. 
3. Utah is super interesting to look at as it was the “reddest state” in the 2012 election but moved toward the center in 2016, I wonder what the next decade will look like for Utah, will there be demographic changes in the state changing the electorate as happened in other red states like Georgia and Arizona. 
4. Many of these states are “flipping” back and forth each election cycle. It is almost more of a “sway” as some of the shifts do not change the outcome of a states election title: “the waves of the shifting electorate”

   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

raw_comment: I noticed that most states stick to what they've previously known for, aside from the outliers. Most states, however, tend to be quite balanced and reflect the concept that no state is truly biased. Although the graph covers less than two decades' worth of data, I wonder if states shift entirely as time passes, as it is seen when Obama won in 2008 compared to Trump in 2016. The impact on my community is minimal, as Illinois is primarily a blue state due to the major cities within it. This does not mean every county is blue-voting, as entire counties are known to be red. Regardless, with the pattern of votes from Illinois, the graph only shows it staying the same while fluctuating in quantity. This graph would be best described as "Parties Shifting per Presidential Election."

raw_comment: I noticed that throughout these past 5 years there have been many shifts in political parties in many states. I also noticed that many states are leaning blue, but from these lines I can also notice that this past election was very close in terms of states leaning blue or red. I wonder what the statistics will be for future elections, considering how close these past two presidential elections have been. I also wonder if within these next 4 years of having a president belonging to the Democratic Party, a new third party will emerge with a candidate that has many supporters, creating a different colored line on the graph. Especially in today’s climate with the younger generation I think people are moving away from the two-party system in favor of more radical change and views. The impact of these statistics on me is that whichever way the country leans in terms of red or blue will determine the president I have for the next 4 years as well as the legislation that president will enact that abides with their party. A headline I would give this article is “Close Call For America, But the Country is Becoming Bluer”.

1. I noticed that the Republican side is much more jumbled up compared to the Democratic side. The area between +10 Rep. and +20 Rep. is very much intersecting. 3.  My community isn't impacted greatly by this because Illinois has been a blue state for a very long time. In other communities, this matters greatly because maybe some communities are from swing states and they are important in presidential elections.

4. Swing Left, Swing Right

| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |

raw_comment:
So in this graph there is a great many things happening. First and foremost I observed the fact that while some states remained the same many also changed drastically either still remaining on their respective side of flipping. This is very interesting because looking at the compared data I am shocked to see states I always thought were one sided actually go to the other.

I wonder why states like these flipped. For example I wonder why Florida flipped was it due to people moving, more voters,etc? I also wonder how close these elections have been because of this data I’m sure there are certain aspects that can be traced back to this graph.

Although this graph doesn’t really have an affect on my community as IL has remained democratic we can see we become less democratic and levitate more towards the middle of the spectrum. However for other states this really affects them as it has changed outcomes of elections with the swing states.

Essentially this graph shows us the way that states voters voted and if they were strong democratic supporters or republican supporters during different presidency’s. The Name of the graph should be 

The Political Balance
How have states party affiliations shifted over the last 5 presidential elections?

raw_comment: I noticed that there was a large shift of states toward the Democratic Party during Obama’s win in 2008. Other than that it seems that most states pretty much stayed with the same party, with only a slight shift of states toward the Republican Party during Trump’s win in 2016. I wonder why there was such a large increase in democratic states from Bush’s election in 2004 to Obama’s election in 2008. I also wonder why, in Obama’s election in 2012, not as many states voted Democrat as in 2008. These elections impact me and my community because the president has the ability to alter the lives of Americans. Depending on where they stand and their policies, they can have a great impact on how certain people live. It’s important to vote and use your voice to choose the candidate that you believe will benefit America because it does make a difference, and staying silent won’t change anything. The graph shows states and which party the majority voted for in the past five elections. A headline could be “States that Changed the Course of Our Elections.”

Also, I noticed that in the 2008 election many states moved closer to the blue side of the graph and then in 2016 those same states that flipped blue switched back to red.

|---|---|---|

| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |

raw_comment:
I noticed that Vermont experienced the greatest shift in voters amongst the democratic states, and Utah experienced the greatest shift in voters amongst the republican states. 

I wonder why this is the case. What change occurred in these states, or rather what acted as a catalyst in the process for which these states gained more democratic or republican voters; was this purely based off of the political candidates, or rather local influencers who rain for local office?

This does not have as large of an impact on me and my community due to the fact that New York has remained democratic for many years. However, this graph does have an impact on me and my community, because the changes which have occurred in other states directly affect which political candidate is chosen.

This graph shows the effect which political candidates have on the voters in the United States; though this may appear to be short-term impacts due to the fact that a presidential term is 4 years, it is in actuality effected the future development of this country.

4 year deception, 50 + year reality

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph shows how the political parties of different states have shifted over the past 5 elections. The graph measures how many representatives each state has and shows the political party that the representatives voted for during each election. To me, it seems like many states swayed to the left during the 2008 election. Perhaps this is because of Barack Obama’s popularity. The graph is a little bit confusing to me because it is difficult to see where each state is listed. I wonder if it is possible for a state to have a tie during a presidential election. This effects my community because the president creates policies which impact the lives of all Americans. In addition, the words of the president can heavily shape the political climate and political attitudes of the people. I wish that America was a true democracy and that the president could be chosen through a popular vote. Unfortunately, the election system is set up in a confusing way which makes it feel like a game.
Headline: Some states are steady, others swing!
